L15: Did you know that:
L16: When 42nd street was closed in New York City, instead of the predicted traffic gridlock, traffic flow actually improved?
L17: or
L18: When a new road was constructed in Stuttgart, Germany, traffic flow worsened and only improved after the road was torn up? These paradoxical phenomena are but two real-life examples of the Braess paradox, named after Dietrich Braess who, in 1968, noted that, in a user-optimized transportation network, when a new link (road) is added, the change in equilibrium flows may result in a higher cost (travel time) to all travelers in the network, implying that users were better off without that link.
